At five, Darshan clung to his mother Vasudha's leg at a housewarming party, his forehead pressed into her sari. When the hostess bent down to greet him, he turned his face away. Vasudha did not push. She stayed by the door with her hand on his shoulder until he loosened his grip and watched the children playing.

At fifteen, Darshan had a long essay for English, due on Friday. He sat in front of his laptop and instead of opening the file, he scrolled through videos. "Every time I think about the file, it looks huge," he muttered to himself. "Ten pages. I'm not able to write ten pages. So I don't even look at it." His stomach felt heavy. On Thursday night he was still scrolling, and the essay was still a shut icon on the screen.

His English teacher Swati asked him after class whether he was stuck. He shrugged, then said, "I keep looking at the whole thing." She suggested he write only the opening paragraph that evening. It seemed small enough to try.

qa.q: Where did Darshan's mother Vasudha stay at the housewarming party?
qa.a: Vasudha stayed by the door with her hand on his shoulder.

qa.q: How is Darshan's avoidance at five like his avoidance at fifteen, and what does gentle help look like each time?
qa.a: At five he avoids the scary greeting by hiding behind Vasudha, and at fifteen he avoids the huge essay by scrolling, since staying away feels like relief; Vasudha's quiet nearness and Swati's suggestion of one small paragraph both make the next step smaller.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when he muttered that the file looks huge?
qa.a: Darshan felt small and overwhelmed by the ten pages, so he avoided even opening the file.

qa.q: What did Swati suggest that could help Darshan begin?
qa.a: Swati suggested he write only the opening paragraph that evening, which shrinks the huge task into something he can try.

grounding: Avoidance in a child hiding at a party, and a teenager whose reasoning shows he avoids a long essay because the size of it makes him feel small.

passage:
At sixteen, Ankita had a chemistry project due in two weeks. She lit her desk lamp each evening, looked at the blank page, and then decided to tidy her drawers instead. If she tried and the model looked poor, her teacher Pranav might see she was not as capable as her marks suggested. Keeping the page blank felt safer. She handed in a hurried project and told nobody how worried she had been.

At twenty-five, at her desk before a client proposal, Ankita felt the same dread creeping back. This time she said to herself, "Just five minutes." Yesterday evening she had laid out her notes and opened the document to the first heading, so it was waiting. She wrote a clumsy paragraph and kept going. When she thought of all the delays in the past, she added, "That was me being scared. It's okay. I'm here now."

Her colleague Tushar looked at her steady typing and asked, "You seem calm today." Ankita smiled. "Small start, kind voice."

qa.q: How long did Ankita commit to when she began the client proposal?
qa.a: Ankita committed to just five minutes.

qa.q: What changed in how Ankita handles a task she is afraid of between sixteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: At sixteen she avoids starting to protect her self-image, and the project suffers; at twenty-five she lays out her notes the night before, commits to five minutes and forgives her past delays, which breaks the dread.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as she tidied her drawers at sixteen?
qa.a: Ankita was afraid that a poor model would show she was not as capable as her marks suggested.

qa.q: Why does forgiving past delays help Ankita begin?
qa.a: Speaking kindly to herself takes away the shame of earlier delays, making it easier to face the next task instead of avoiding it.

grounding: Procrastination linked across ages: a teenager avoiding judgement by not starting, and a young professional who breaks the dread with a tiny start and self-compassion.

passage:
At five, Sumit lay on the rug and groaned, "I'm bored. Can I watch cartoons?" His mother Leela had a basket of old spoons, cups and a bowl of water ready. "Try a kitchen for your toys," she said. Sumit sighed, then began pouring, stirring and inviting his teddy to tea. He did not mention the cartoons again until dinner.

At fifteen, on a Sunday evening, Sumit noticed that he had spent nearly the whole weekend on videos and games. He felt a flash of shame, then stopped and took out a notebook. "What happened?" On Saturday he had argued with his friend Tanuja, and by afternoon there had been nothing else to do. He wrote: "Fight, then bored, then screen." He did not call himself hopeless.

Instead he texted Tanuja to fix the quarrel and asked her to go cycling the following Saturday. On Monday morning he put his phone on the shelf during homework and started again from there.

qa.q: What was in Leela's basket when Sumit said he was bored?
qa.a: The basket held old spoons, cups and a bowl of water.

qa.q: How do the two moments show different ways of handling boredom in Sumit's life?
qa.a: At five boredom is answered by simple materials that let him invent a kitchen, and at fifteen he reviews a weekend binge, finds the triggers of the fight and boredom, plans a cycling outing and restarts on Monday without self-blame.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling on Sunday evening when he noticed the weekend had gone to screens?
qa.a: Sumit felt a flash of shame, but he steadied himself and looked for the cause instead of blaming himself.

qa.q: What did Sumit change so the next weekend would go differently?
qa.a: He mended the quarrel with Tanuja and planned a cycling trip, which gave the weekend something to do besides screens.

grounding: Boredom in a young child answered by simple materials, and the same person later reviewing a screen-heavy weekend, spotting the argument and boredom behind it, and restarting kindly.

passage:
At nine, Deepak lost his place while reading aloud and the class began to giggle. He waggled his ears, crossed his eyes and said, "Ladies and gentlemen, the world's slowest reader!" The class cheered. He kept the room laughing until the bell, though he chewed his lip as he sat down.

At twenty-one, during an internship at an engineering firm, Deepak was told to sign off a test log without running the last check. "Just tick it, nobody looks," a colleague said. Deepak said, "I'd love to, but I don't want the bridge to fall on my head in my sleep." Two colleagues laughed, but one muttered, "You're too sincere. Not practical."

Deepak said he would run the check quickly, and did it in ten minutes. He did not lecture anyone. Later Chandrika, a junior engineer, found him at the coffee machine. "I'm glad you didn't tick it," she said. Wasim, from the lab, joined them the next day, and the three began running the checks together and sharing the load.

qa.q: What did Deepak say to the class when he lost his place reading aloud?
qa.a: He said, "Ladies and gentlemen, the world's slowest reader!"

qa.q: How does Deepak's use of humour at nine differ from his use of humour at twenty-one?
qa.a: At nine the joke keeps control after a stumble and hides his embarrassment, while at twenty-one it lets him refuse a shortcut without a lecture, and then he gains allies in Chandrika and Wasim.

qa.q: What was Deepak probably feeling when a colleague called him too sincere?
qa.a: Deepak felt the sting of being mocked for his integrity, though he answered lightly and stayed with his choice.

qa.q: What did Deepak do that helped him keep his line without turning self-righteous?
qa.a: He joked about it, ran the check quickly and did not lecture, so he held his position with humour and skill, and then found allies.

grounding: Humour used to cover embarrassment in childhood and later used with skill to hold a line against a shortcut when colleagues mock integrity as too sincere.

passage:
At five, Suraj lay across the armchair with his legs over the arm. "I'm bored. What can I do? Can I have the tablet?" His father Imran did not hand it over. He put an empty egg carton and some clay on the floor and said, "I wonder what these want to be." Suraj rolled his eyes, then made twelve tiny clay birds and lined them up in the carton.

At fifteen, Suraj sat on the bed and scrolled, switching from a video app to a chat, then to a game, then back again, thumb flicking through the same feed twice. His sister Noor looked in. "You've been doing that for an hour," she said. "Are you even watching anything?" Suraj paused. "No. It's like... if I stop, it's just empty." He put the phone face down on the pillow and sat still. The flat feeling rose, uncomfortable but bearable, and after a few minutes he picked up his guitar instead.

qa.q: How many clay birds did Suraj make at five?
qa.a: Suraj made twelve tiny clay birds.

qa.q: How do Suraj's boredom at five and at fifteen resemble each other, and how do they differ?
qa.a: Both begin with a restless feeling of having nothing to do; at five simple materials from Imran turn it into clay birds, while at fifteen scrolling avoids the empty moment, and Suraj learns he can sit with the flat feeling and then choose the guitar.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he told Noor that if he stopped it was just empty?
qa.a: Suraj felt uneasy at the empty moment, which he had been trying to escape by scrolling.

qa.q: What did Noor do that helped Suraj notice his habit?
qa.a: Noor pointed out that he had been scrolling for an hour and asked if he was watching anything, which made Suraj pause and say what he felt.

grounding: Boredom at two ages: a young child's restlessness turned into play, and a teenager's compulsive scrolling that avoids an empty moment.

passage:
At five, Karthik hid behind his father Akash's legs at every party and would not say hello. Akash stayed near and let him watch, and by the end of the evening Karthik would wave from a distance.

At fifteen, Karthik began to miss things. First the school trip ("I have a headache"), then a cousin's wedding ("too tired"), then a friend's birthday ("a lot of homework"). His parents saw the pattern but each time accepted the excuse, wanting to keep the evening peaceful. Akash even phoned the friend's mother to say Karthik couldn't come. Karthik's world grew smaller each month.

One evening Akash sat down beside him. "We've been letting you skip things because we didn't want you to be upset," he said. "That wasn't fair to you. Could we try one small thing, like coming to the birthday for half an hour with me waiting outside?" Karthik was silent. His father added gently, "And we can talk to Francis, the school counsellor, together." Karthik gave a small nod.

qa.q: What excuse did Karthik give for the school trip?
qa.a: Karthik said he had a headache.

qa.q: How does Akash's response when Karthik is five differ from the parents' response when Karthik is fifteen?
qa.a: At five Akash stays near and lets Karthik watch, which gently helps him warm up; at fifteen the parents accept every excuse to keep the peace and Karthik's world shrinks, until Akash proposes one small step and the counsellor, instead of either pushing or rescuing.

qa.q: What might Karthik be feeling when he offers excuses for the trip and the wedding?
qa.a: Karthik is probably afraid of the event and seeks relief by staying away, which feeds his fear.

qa.q: What did Akash do that could help Karthik move forward?
qa.a: Akash admitted the excuses had not helped, suggested one small step of half an hour with support waiting outside, and offered to see the counsellor Francis together.

grounding: Avoidance in a child hiding at parties and a teenager whose missed events are accepted by parents until a parent offers a small step and counsellor support.
